197 FERC ¶ 61,086
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER DENYING APPLICATION FOR AUTHORIZATION OF DISPOSITION OF JURISDICTIONAL FACILITIES AND DISMISSING PETITION FOR DECLARATORY ORDER

(Issued November 2, 2026)

On November 7, 2025, as amended June 29, 2026, pursuant to section 203 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and Part 33 of the Commission’s regulations, PacifiCorp  filed an application (Application) requesting approval of a proposed sale-leaseback transaction (Proposed Transaction) involving PacifiCorp’s ownership interest in the Boardman-to -Hemingway Transmission Project (B2H Project).  PacifiCorp states that the Proposed Transaction is a “standard” sale-leaseback financing involving the sale of PacifiCorp’s rights to the B2H Project to a passive, affiliated special-purpose lessor   (SPE Lessor) and the subsequent leaseback of such rights in the B2H Project to PacifiCorp.  In its petition for declaratory order, PacifiCorp requests that the Commission determine that SPE Lessor will not, as a result of the Proposed Transaction, be considered a “public utility” under section 201(e) of the FPA.
We have reviewed the Proposed Transaction under the Commission’s Merger Policy Statement.  As discussed below, we deny, without prejudice, authorization for the Proposed Transaction because we find that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate on the record of this proceeding that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on rates.  We also dismiss as moot the petition for declaratory order.
Background
Description of PacifiCorp and Relevant Entities
PacifiCorp
PacifiCorp states that it is a vertically integrated public utility primarily engaged in providing retail electric service to residential, commercial, industrial, and other customers in portions of California, Idaho, Oregon, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming.  PacifiCorp further states that it provides open access transmission service under its Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT), which is on file with the Commission, and operates an integrated transmission system spanning two balancing authority areas – PacifiCorp East and PacifiCorp West.  PacifiCorp states that it is regulated by the following state public utility commissions:  the Utah Public Service Commission (Utah Commission), the Oregon Public Utility Commission (Oregon Commission), the Wyoming Public Service Commission (Wyoming Commission), the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission (Washington Commission), the Idaho Public Utilities Commission (Idaho Commission), and the California Public Utilities Commission (California Commission).
PacifiCorp represents that it is an indirect, wholly owned subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway Energy Company (Berkshire Hathaway), which is a holding company that owns subsidiaries principally engaged in the energy business and is itself a consolidated, wholly owned subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway Inc., a publicly traded corporation.
SPE Lessor
PacifiCorp states that SPE Lessor, the buyer/lessor in the Proposed Transaction, is a special purpose entity established by Berkshire Hathaway for the purpose of acquiring the B2H Project and leasing the B2H Project back to PacifiCorp.  PacifiCorp represents that SPE Lessor is a wholly owned subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway and does not own or control any Commission jurisdictional assets.  PacifiCorp states that pursuant to the Proposed Transaction, SPE Lessor’s interest in the B2H Project will be that of a traditional passive lessor.  Accordingly, PacifiCorp asserts that SPE Lessor is not a public utility under section 201(e) of the FPA and will not become a public utility under section 201(e) of the FPA following the consummation of the Proposed Transaction, and PacifiCorp requests that the Commission confirm as much in its petition for declaratory order, as described below.
The B2H Project
PacifiCorp explains that the B2H Project is currently under construction by PacifiCorp and Idaho Power Company (Idaho Power) and that both will be a           tenant-in-common owner in the B2H Project and jointly serve the capacity created by the B2H Project.  PacifiCorp also states that the B2H Project will be a 300-mile long, 500 kilovolt (kV) electric transmission line in the Pacific Northwest.  It states that the B2H Project will deliver up to 1,000 megawatts of power in each direction, helping utilities meet customer demand, especially during the Pacific Northwest’s winter peak and the Mountain West’s summer peak.  Additionally, PacifiCorp states that the B2H Project will provide a second transmission connection between PacifiCorp East and PacifiCorp West, which are currently connected only by the Midpoint-to-Summer Lake 500 kV transmission line.  PacifiCorp states that the B2H Project is expected to be in service by late 2027.
PacifiCorp explains that dating back to 2010, PacifiCorp and Idaho Power have filed several agreements necessary to facilitate construction of the B2H Project:  the B2H Construction Funding Agreement (Construction Funding Agreement), Joint Purchase and Sale Agreement between PacifiCorp and Idaho Power (Purchase and Sale Agreement) and the B2H Joint Ownership and Operating Agreement (Ownership and Operating Agreement).  PacifiCorp represents that these agreements are each necessary components for Idaho Power and PacifiCorp to serve increasing demand on their respective systems.  PacifiCorp states that through these agreements, it has contractual obligations to fund its share of the B2H Project. 
Description of the Proposed Transaction
PacifiCorp states that the Proposed Transaction is a sale-leaseback transaction pursuant to which PacifiCorp will convey to SPE Lessor its tenant-in-common interests in the B2H Project and immediately take leasehold rights in the B2H Project as lessee.  PacifiCorp explains that a sale-leaseback is generally used to provide the seller-lessee access to cash from their owned assets while retaining the use of those assets for operations.  PacifiCorp states that under the Proposed Transaction, it retains complete leasehold interests in the B2H Project and will maintain the same control of its B2H Project rights and capacity as it has today.  It further states that the B2H Project will be located in the Idaho Power balancing authority area and Idaho Power Company has been designated to be the operator of the B2H Project under the Ownership and Operating Agreement once the B2H Project is in service.
PacifiCorp states that the Proposed Transaction will be effectuated through two agreements:  the Master Purchase and Sale Agreement (Purchase Agreement) and the Master Lease Agreement (Lease Agreement).  It explains that, together with the schedule for the B2H Project, the Purchase Agreement governs the purchase and sale of the B2H Project and the Lease Agreement forms the terms and conditions for the lease of the tenant-in-common interests in the B2H Project.
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of the Application was published in the Federal Register, with interventions and protests due on or before December 8, 2025.  A timely motion to intervene and protest was filed by the Wyoming Industrial Energy Consumers (Wyoming Consumers).
On December 23, 2025, PacifiCorp filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to Wyoming Consumers’ protest (PacifiCorp Answer).
On March 6, 2026, PacifiCorp submitted a notice to the Commission that the Oregon Commission approved the Proposed Transaction on March 3, 2026 and provided a copy of the ruling.
On May 6, 2026, the Commission issued an order pursuant to FPA section 203(a)(5) tolling the time for action on the Application for 180 days.
On May 21, 2026, a deficiency letter was issued (Deficiency Letter) seeking additional information on the Proposed Transaction.  On June 18, 2026, PacifiCorp requested an extension of time to respond to the Deficiency Letter, which was granted.  On June 29, 2026, PacifiCorp filed its response to the Deficiency Letter (Deficiency Letter Response).
Notice of the Deficiency Letter Response was published in the Federal Register, with interventions and protests due on or before July 20, 2026.  None was filed.
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,        18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the timely, unopposed motion to intervene serves to make Wyoming Consumers a party to this proceeding.
Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the PacifiCorp Answer because it has provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
Proposed Transaction
FPA Section 203 Standard of Review
FPA section 203(a)(4) requires the Commission to approve proposed dispositions, consolidations, acquisitions, or changes in control if the Commission determines that the proposed transaction will be consistent with the public interest.  The Commission’s analysis of whether a proposed transaction is consistent with the public interest generally involves consideration of three factors:  (1) the effect on competition; (2) the effect on rates; and (3) the effect on regulation.  FPA section 203(a)(4) also requires the Commission to find that the proposed transaction “will not result in cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company, unless the Commission determines that the cross-subsidization, pledge, or encumbrance will be consistent with the public interest.”  The Commission’s regulations establish verification and informational requirements for entities that seek a determination that a proposed transaction will not result in inappropriate cross-subsidization or pledge or encumbrance of utility assets.
As discussed below, we deny, without prejudice, authorization for the Proposed Transaction because we find that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate on the record of this proceeding that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on rates.  For this reason, we do not address the other public interest factors of the FPA section 203 analysis.  Because we deny authorization of the Proposed Transaction, we also need not address Wyoming Consumers’ protest regarding the Proposed Transaction’s effect on regulation. 
Analysis of the Proposed Transaction
Effect on Rates
PacifiCorp’s Analysis
PacifiCorp states that as a transmission asset transaction, no wholesale power rates will be impacted by the Proposed Transaction.  With respect to transmission rates, PacifiCorp states that it has a formula transmission rate on file with the Commission that is updated on an annual basis.
PacifiCorp states that the primary impact of the Proposed Transaction on transmission rates will be to change the manner in which PacifiCorp recovers its investment.  PacifiCorp states that under the Proposed Transaction, PacifiCorp will make quarterly lease payments to SPE Lessor that will be levelized for the 20-year term of the lease, and that will be passed through transmission rates as an expense.  PacifiCorp states that the lease payments will be calculated using a formula that estimates the net present value of the payment stream that customers would pay for the B2H Project using traditional ratemaking and sets the lease payment on the same basis (Lease Payment Methodology).  PacifiCorp states that the Lease Payment Methodology calculates the quarterly lease payment by first calculating a traditional revenue requirement over the 20-year lease term.  It states that the operations and maintenance expenses that PacifiCorp may incur will not be incurred by or paid to SPE Lessor but instead will be passed through the formula rate as expense in the same manner as they would in the absence of the Proposed Transaction.  PacifiCorp states that the quarterly lease payment is then calculated in a manner to ensure that the net present value of the lease payments over the 20-year term does not exceed the net present value of the total payments under the traditional method.  PacifiCorp states that, in this way, the lease payments are structured to effectively mimic traditional ratemaking, with the exception of the use of levelized recovery and the time value of money that results from shifting the timing of those payments.  PacifiCorp states that PacifiCorp and SPE Lessor will calculate the lease payment based on the lower of PacifiCorp’s then-governing regulated weighted average cost of capital (WACC) from either its OATT formula rate or the average of its state-approved WACC in retail cases across its various state jurisdictions at the time of the closing of the Proposed Transaction.  PacifiCorp asserts that this approach to the rate of return will ensure that the PacifiCorp OATT and retail customers do not pay a higher rate of return for the B2H Project than they would under traditional ratemaking.
PacifiCorp states that the exact lease payment amount will not be known until the closing of the Proposed Transaction, and until the total amount of PacifiCorp’s investment in the B2H Project and the total amount of payments received from SPE Lessor are known.
PacifiCorp argues that the Commission has endorsed the use of levelized rates for single asset transmission investments due to offsetting benefits.  PacifiCorp asserts that levelized payments will affirmatively benefit customers in the early years of the operational life of the B2H Project, when compared to the impact of including PacifiCorp’s billion-dollar-plus investment in plant accounts upon the commercial operation date of the B2H Project.  PacifiCorp argues that levelizing charges in this manner is simply a matter of the timing of cost recovery; it does not change the amount of invested capital that would be recovered through rates over time.
PacifiCorp states that it is separately filing the Lease Agreement, which contains the Lease Payment Methodology, under section 205 of the FPA.
Deficiency Letter and Response
The Deficiency Letter requested, among other things, that PacifiCorp describe how the Proposed Transaction will affect transmission rates by year and compare the proposed lease payment to the transmission rate customers would pay for the B2H Project using traditional ratemaking.  In the Deficiency Letter Response, PacifiCorp reiterates the explanation in the Application, stating that the lease payment methodology in the Lease Agreement would achieve the same results as traditional ratemaking over the lease term, except using the levelized nature of lease expense recovery.  PacifiCorp also provides illustrative numbers and inputs to demonstrate how the lease payment calculations would work and asserts that that information shows that the net present value of the payment customers would pay for the B2H Project over a 20-year window using traditional ratemaking and compared with the total levelized lease payments calculated for the same 20-year window, are “virtually identical.”
The Deficiency Letter also requested additional information regarding rates under PacifiCorp’s levelized approach.  In particular, the Deficiency Letter requested that PacifiCorp identify and explain whether there are any offsetting benefits resulting from the Proposed Transaction.  The Deficiency Letter also requested information regarding any potential ratepayer protections.  In response, PacifiCorp states that the effect of the levelized lease payments, which are lower than under traditional ratemaking in the short run and higher in the long run, “offset one another.”  Further, PacifiCorp states that customers will benefit from PacifiCorp choosing the lower of its weighted average cost of capital in setting the return on equity.  PacifiCorp also states that customers will benefit from the stability in recovery under its levelized lease payment approach, and that the primary rate assurances for customers under the Lease Agreement are transparency and certainty.
Wyoming Consumers’ Protest
Wyoming Consumers argue that PacifiCorp incorrectly assumes that the B2H Project would be placed into rate base upon commercial operation, but the B2H Project was removed from PacifiCorp’s preferred portfolio in its 2025 Integrated Resource Plan based on the B2H Project’s inability to serve native load, and based on the understanding that large load customers would be expected to pay for its costs.
Wyoming Consumers explain that PacifiCorp’s transmission customers, including Rocky Mountain Power, pay for transmission and ancillary services through PacifiCorp’s transmission formula rate, which is updated by PacifiCorp’s annual transmission service.  They state that this includes all transmission system investments made by PacifiCorp, a return on rate base, income taxes, expenses, and certain revenue credits, among other specific elements and adjustments.  Wyoming Consumers further state that once the annual transmission revenue requirement is assessed against PacificCorp’s transmission customers, a portion of PacifiCorp’s transmission revenues are credited to PacifiCorp’s state retail customers.  They explain that under this approach, PacifiCorp allocates 100% of its transmission costs to both state retail and Commission jurisdictional customers.  Wyoming Consumers state that the Commission, through PacifiCorp’s annual transmission revenue requirements, determines the appropriate amount to be recovered from PacifiCorp’s wholesale customers.  They state that this same amount is then credited to PacifiCorp’s retail customers as a deduction to PacifiCorp’s retail cost of service.
Wyoming Consumers further assert that when PacifiCorp obtained a Non-Situs Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity from the Wyoming Commission to construct the B2H Project, the Wyoming Commission stated that the approval was in part “‘based upon necessity to the system as a whole,’” and that its order “‘does not determine any ratemaking issues, all of which are expressly reserved for future decision in appropriate proceedings before the [c]ommission.  This includes any future cost recovery or any future cost allocation arrangements associated with the [B2H Project].’”
Wyoming Consumers state that PacifiCorp subsequently removed the B2H Project from its preferred portfolio and provided two reasons for the removal:  (1) new large load customers, not PacifiCorp’s general retail customers would be expected to provide or pay for the necessary resources and transmission to serve their load; and (2) that PacifiCorp was unable to use the B2H Project to move network resources to load.  Wyoming Consumers contend that these representations contradict PacifiCorp’s assumption in this proceeding that there are no adverse effects on rates because the B2H Project will be placed into rate base upon commercial operation.
Wyoming Consumers argue that the Wyoming Commission currently has jurisdiction over whether PacifiCorp can recover B2H Project costs in retail rates, but it is unclear whether the Wyoming Commission would retain that jurisdiction if the Commission approves the Proposed Transaction.  They request a hearing or conditional approval of the Proposed Transaction and request that the Commission state that its approval is made without prejudice to the authority of any state regulatory body with respect to rates, service, accounts, valuation, estimates or determination of costs.  
PacifiCorp Answer
PacifiCorp argues that Wyoming Consumers raise essentially a single issue:  the standard of review that should apply to a future retail rate case seeking cost recovery for the B2H Project from Wyoming retail customers and which retail customer class should pay for the line.  It contends that the Commission should not consider this issue because PacifiCorp has not yet sought cost recovery of any investment in the B2H Project from Wyoming retail customers and has not asked the Commission to make any findings of law in this regard.  PacifiCorp maintains that Wyoming Consumers are asking for a premature and speculative declaratory ruling that the Commission’s approval of the Proposed Transaction under section 203 will not impact the cost recovery review of the Wyoming Commission.  It provides four reasons why the Commission should reject Wyoming Consumers’ request:  (1) Wyoming Consumers’ concern is unduly vague;     (2) the concerns are premature and beyond the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction; (3) the “effect on rates” concerns fall well short of establishing an adverse impact on rates; and (4) Wyoming Consumers’ request for hearing are unfounded and based on speculative legal issues that cannot be resolved by hearing or settlement procedures.
PacifiCorp argues that the Wyoming Commission will continue to retain jurisdiction over PacifiCorp’s retail rates and that Wyoming Consumers are essentially asking for a premature determination on one specific line item in a future Wyoming retail rate case.
Commission Determination
We deny, without prejudice, PacifiCorp’s request for authorization of the Proposed Transaction.  We emphasize at the outset that our analysis of rate effects under FPA section 203 differs from the analysis we apply to determine whether rates are just and reasonable under FPA section 205.  Our focus here is on the effect that the Proposed Transaction will have on rates; whether that effect is adverse; and whether any adverse effect will be mitigated or offset by benefits that are likely to result from the Proposed Transaction.  Where applicants expect an effect on rates, applicants typically disclose and discuss that effect in their section 203 applications and attempt to demonstrate that an adverse effect on rates will be mitigated or offset by benefits.
Based on our review of the record in this proceeding, we conclude that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate on the record of this proceeding that the Proposed Transaction will not result in an adverse effect on rates or that the benefits of the Proposed Transaction are sufficient to offset such adverse effect on rates.  
PacifiCorp provided illustrative numbers for the lease payment methodology in the Deficiency Letter Response to support its assertion that the net present value of the lease payments under levelized ratemaking does not exceed the net present value of the total payments under traditional ratemaking.  However, we find that PacifiCorp’s net present value equivalency does not provide assurance that rates will be unchanged by the Proposed Transaction and that that effect on rates would not be adverse because the nominal dollar amount of the total lease payments collected under the proposed levelized approach would be higher than the total payments that would have been collected under traditional ratemaking.  Under PacifiCorp’s hypothetical example, the total payments for ratepayers under the levelized lease payment approach is projected to be over $95 million more over the 20-year term of the lease than under the traditional ratemaking approach.  Accordingly, we find that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate on the record of this proceeding that its proposed levelized approach for the lease payments will not result in an adverse effect on rates.    
With respect to offsetting benefits, PacifiCorp asserts that as is the expected result of a levelized approach, levelized costs are lower than traditional ratemaking in the short run and higher in the long run.  Further, PacifiCorp asserts that customers will benefit from the stability in recovery of the B2H Project, and the “lower of approach” in setting the return on equity.  However, these features of the levelized approach could also be considered adverse to customers, such that the purported benefits may also create an adverse effect on rates resulting from the Proposed Transaction.  For example, during the later part of the lease term, customers will pay levelized rates that are higher than they would have paid under traditional ratemaking.  In any event, as indicated above, we find that customers will pay higher rates under the Proposed Transaction under levelized ratemaking than under traditional ratemaking.  PacifiCorp’s arguments as to the benefits of a levelized approach versus traditional ratemaking do not overcome that finding.  
For these reasons, we find that PacifiCorp has failed to show that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on rates or that the benefits of the Proposed Transaction are sufficient to offset such adverse effect on rates.  Accordingly, we deny, without prejudice, authorization of the Proposed Transaction.  PacifiCorp may file a new application pursuant to FPA section 203 that either provides the requisite demonstration that its proposal does not have an adverse effect on rates or proposes adequate ratepayer protections or demonstrates specific additional benefits to offset the rate increase.  Should PacifiCorp choose to refile, it may consider providing sufficient support for potential offsetting benefits, which the Commission would evaluate based on the record in the subsequent filing, such as benefits associated with preventing rate shock or providing financing flexibility that may help ensure the project is completed and lead to lower costs for customers.  Additionally, PacifiCorp may consider proposing to mitigate the effect on rates by agreeing to a lower net present value, which may result in sharing the potential benefits of this financing mechanism with customers.  The Commission will evaluate any future filing at that time.  
In response to Wyoming Consumers, we find that concern regarding the removal of the B2H Project from PacifiCorp’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan is beyond the scope of the Commission’s evaluation of a proposed transaction’s effect on rates.  Further, we note that approval of any future application is without prejudice to the authority of the Commission or any other regulatory body with respect to rates, service, accounts, valuation, estimates, or determinations of costs. 
Accounting Analysis
PacifiCorp requests approval of its proposed use of lease accounting.  After the B2H Project is completed and transferred to SPE Lessor, PacifiCorp proposes to remove the project from Account 107 (Construction Work in Progress—Electric) and recognize a right-of-use asset in Account 101.1 (Property under Capital Leases), with corresponding lease liabilities in Account 227 (Obligations under Capital Leases—Noncurrent) and Account 243 (Obligations under Capital Leases—Current) to account for the sale-leaseback transaction, reflecting its ongoing operational control related to the project.
Additionally, to ensure that rental expenses align with the proposed levelized   cost-of-service recovery, PacifiCorp proposes to transfer the quarterly rental expenses from Account 567 (Rents) to Account 182.3 (Other Regulatory Assets), allowing for amortization that matches transmission ratemaking over the 20-year lease term.  Although using a regulatory asset to record costs in support of a levelized cost-of-service may be appropriate, PacifiCorp must seek regulatory approval under section 205 of the FPA to include the levelized amortization of the regulatory asset in transmission rates.
Request for Disclaimer of Jurisdiction
In its petition for declaratory order, PacifiCorp seeks confirmation that, as a result of the consummation of the Proposed Transaction, SPE Lessor will not be considered a “public utility” under FPA section 201(e).  PacifiCorp asserts that because it will remain in control of its interests in the B2H Project pursuant to its OATT and the other B2H agreements already on file with the Commission, there is no need to assert public utility jurisdiction over the passive SPE Lessor.
Because PacifiCorp’s request is tied to the authorization of the Proposed Transaction, which we deny without prejudice in this order, PacifiCorp’s request that the Commission disclaim jurisdiction over SPE Lessor is dismissed as moot.
The Commission orders:
The Application is hereby denied, without prejudice, as discussed in the body of this order. 

PacifiCorp’s petition for declaratory order is hereby dismissed as moot, as discussed in the body of this order.
By the Commission.  Commissioner Rosner is dissenting with a separate statement
 			  attached.
			  Commissioner Chang is dissenting with a separate statement 
  attached.

( S E A L )



Debbie-Anne A. Reese,
Secretary.

FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



(Issued November 2, 2026)

ROSNER, Commissioner, dissenting: 

I dissent from today’s order denying authorization for a proposed transaction to implement a sale-leaseback that would facilitate capital investment in the B2H Project, a 300-mile, 500 kV transmission line that has been in the works since 2010.  
The order concludes that PacifiCorp failed to demonstrate that the proposed transaction would not have an adverse effect on rates but does so by comparing total nominal payments over 20 years, ignoring the real and well understood fact that a dollar today is more valuable than a dollar in 20 years.  The correct basis to make such a comparison is the net present value, which allows us to compare two different payment schedules over time in real dollars, accounting for the time value of money. 
Here, PacifiCorp did exactly that and demonstrated that the real difference between the total revenue it will collect from customers under the proposed transaction and under the status quo is zero.  The chart below, showing data filed in the record from PacifiCorp, shows how the proposed transaction would reduce annual costs in the near term in exchange for higher costs in later years, holding customers harmless on a net present value basis.  
 
Source: PacifiCorp, June 29, 2026 Response to Deficiency Letter, Att. 1.
I believe PacifiCorp’s analysis is sufficient for the Commission to find that the transaction would not have an adverse effect on rates.  This filing was submitted nearly a year ago and PacifiCorp provided assurances that the post-transaction levelized rate structure carries benefits by ensuring price certainty, improving transparency, and locking in the lower of federal and state rates of return on equity for customers.  It is unclear what more could be needed to support a proposal like the one PacifiCorp makes here.  
For these reasons, I respectfully dissent.
________________________

David Rosner
Commissioner



UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



(Issued November 2, 2026)

CHANG, Commissioner, dissenting: 

In companion orders issued today, the Commission rejects Federal Power Act (FPA) section 203 and 205 filings from PacifiCorp that implement a proposed sale-leaseback and accompanying levelized rate proposal to facilitate a capital investment in the Boardman-to-Hemingway Transmission Project (B2H Project).  I dissent from both orders because I believe PacifiCorp has satisfied its burdens under FPA sections 203 and 205 to demonstrate, as relevant here, that its proposed levelized rate proposal does not create an adverse effect on rates and is otherwise just and reasonable.
Overview of Levelized Rates versus Traditional Cost of Service Rates
The decision before the Commission in these proceedings turns largely on the differences between a traditional cost of service (COS) rate design and a levelized rate design.  Under traditional COS ratemaking, the revenue requirement associated with an individual capital asset declines over time.  Specifically, as a capital asset depreciates, the regulated return – which is a major component of the total rate – decreases, leading to higher rates in the early years of the asset’s life and lower rates in the later years.
By comparison, a levelized rate flattens these payments into equal installments over time, similar to a fixed-rate mortgage.  As compared to a declining traditional COS rate for a specific capital asset, customers with levelized rates pay comparatively less in the early years and more in the outer years, with the utility recovering the same investment over the same period of time.  This alternate payment structure can benefit customers by, for example, reducing rate shock associated with large capital investments as they enter service.  The total nominal amount of costs associated with a levelized rate – not adjusted for the time value of money (e.g., paying a dollar today is costs more to the customer than paying a dollar in five years) – generally exceeds the total nominal amount of a traditional COS rate approach.  
While the two rate structures involve different nominal dollar recovery and distribution of the rate recovery over a common period of time (e.g., 20 years), utilities can set the levelized rates based on equal net present value (NPV) of the traditional COS rates.  NPV-based assessments and rate setting are common in the financial and utility sectors.  NPV-based rate design accounts for the time value of money by setting levelized rates in a manner that is financially equivalent to the front-loaded traditional COS rate, providing ratepayers with lower rates in the early years (when their money is worth more) and higher rates in the out years (when their money is worth less).  This approach can achieve the benefits of a levelized rate design while holding both the utility and its customers harmless compared to a traditional COS rate.        
PacifiCorp’s Proposals and Today’s Orders
As explained in the orders, PacifiCorp submitted three filings to facilitate a capital investment in the B2H Project by a passive special-purpose entity (SPE Lessor) that is affiliated with PacifiCorp: (1) an FPA section 203 application requesting approval of a proposed sale-leaseback involving PacifiCorp’s ownership interest in the B2H Project (Proposed Transaction); (2) a 20-year Master Lease Agreement (Lease Agreement) between PacifiCorp and SPE Lessor, submitted under FPA section 205, which governs the rates, terms, and conditions through which PacifiCorp will lease transmission capacity on the B2H Project; and (3) a petition for declaratory order (Petition) requesting that the Commission affirm that SPE Lessor will not, as a result of the Proposed Transaction, be considered a public utility under section 201(e) of the FPA.  
To recover SPE Lessor’s investment in the B2H Project, the Lease Agreement provides that PacifiCorp will pay SPE Lessor a levelized rate designed to mimic the return of, and on, the investment in the B2H Project that customers would pay under traditional ratemaking.  For purposes of the Commission’s FPA section 203 analysis, the Proposed Transaction’s potential rate effect is the potential difference between this levelized rate structure and the traditional COS rate that PacifiCorp would otherwise charge its customers for the B2H Project.
In the B2H 203 Order, the Commission denies, without prejudice, PacifiCorp’s requested FPA 203 authorization for the Proposed Transaction.  Specifically, the B2H 203 Order finds that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate that its proposed levelized rate structure will not have an adverse effect on rates or that the benefits of the proposed transaction are sufficient to offset an adverse effect.  The B2H 203 Order also dismisses PacifiCorp’s Petition as moot, given its rejection of the Proposed Transaction.  In the B2H 205 Order, the Commission finds that PacifiCorp has not demonstrated that the Lease Agreement is just and reasonable because it does not include a “final, populated project-specific schedule in Exhibit 1 for the B2H Project, including the final lease payment amount, SPE Lessor’s cost, and the net book value of the B2H Project….”  
PacifiCorp Has Adequately Justified Its Levelized Rate Proposal
As discussed below, I disagree with the orders’ conclusion that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate that its Proposed Transaction and levelized rate construct satisfy the requirements of FPA sections 203 and 205.  In particular, PacifiCorp has provided sufficient detail to demonstrate that its proposed levelized rate is reasonably designed and will be equivalent to a traditional COS rate on an NPV basis.  Consequently, its proposed levelized rate does not represent an adverse “effect on rates” and thus satisfies the requirements of FPA section 203.  
PacifiCorp’s Proposed Levelized Rate Structure Is Well-Designed and Will Not Create an Adverse Effect on Rates
The Proposed Transaction raises an issue of first impression regarding how the Commission should assess levelized rate structures under FPA section 203.  As the B2H 203 Order explains, the Commission’s “focus here is on the effect that the Proposed Transaction will have on rates; whether that effect is adverse; and whether any adverse effect will be mitigated or offset by benefits that are likely to result from the Proposed Transaction.”  
I am persuaded based on the record before us that PacifiCorp’s proposed levelized rate structure will not result in an adverse effect on rates.  Broadly, PacifiCorp proposes first to calculate the traditional COS revenue requirement for each year of the 20-year Lease Agreement.  PacifiCorp then proposes to convert that amount to its NPV by applying a discount rate equal to the after-tax weighted average cost of capital (WACC) – recognizing that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today.  It then converts that aggregate 20-year NPV amount into a levelized rate, again relying on the WACC discount rate.  Based on my review of the records, PacifiCorp’s levelized rate design is economically sound and well-supported, using reasonable assumptions for key inputs and demonstrating via calculations how it will ensure the levelized rate is equivalent on an NPV-basis to a traditional COS rate.  While PacifiCorp’s levelized rate yields a nominal difference of $95 million over the life of the 20-year lease, about 5.5% of the total nominal revenue requirement under the traditional COS rate, this is a result of the NPV calculation and the different periods over which the investment is recovered; it is not an adverse rate effect.  Rather, accounting for the timing of recovery, PacifiCorp has demonstrated that the levelized rate is equivalent to a traditional COS rate for both PacifiCorp and its customers.  
Accordingly, I am persuaded that PacifiCorp’s levelized rate proposal provides sufficient protection for customers over the 20-year term of the Lease Agreement, does not create an adverse rate effect under our FPA section 203 framework, and is just and reasonable under FPA section 205.  Unfortunately, as discussed further below, the B2H 203 and 205 Orders reach a different conclusion.  
The Orders Unnecessarily Undermine the Use of Levelized Rates
Instead of accepting PacifiCorp’s well-reasoned rate design, today’s orders conclude that PacifiCorp has failed to demonstrate that its levelized rate proposal satisfies the requirements of FPA sections 203 and 205.  The logic of today’s orders (particularly the B2H 203 Order) creates a significant hurdle for the use of levelized rates in Commission ratemaking.
 The B2H 203 Order finds that PacifiCorp’s NPV “equivalency does not provide assurance that rates will be unchanged by the Proposed Transaction and that that effect on rates would not be adverse because the nominal dollar amount of the total lease payments collected under the proposed levelized approach would be higher than the total payments that would have been collected under traditional ratemaking.”  The B2H 203 Order then dismisses PacifiCorp’s effort to demonstrate offsetting benefits, concluding that (1) the “stability in recovery of the B2H Project, and the ‘lower of approach’ in setting the return on equity…could also be considered adverse to customers,” and (2) any cited benefits “of a levelized approach versus traditional ratemaking” do not overcome the “higher rates under the Proposed Transaction under levelized ratemaking than under traditional ratemaking.”  The B2H 205 Order rejects the Lease Agreement, concluding that, notwithstanding the detail PacifiCorp provides regarding how its lease payment will ultimately be derived, the Commission cannot assess whether it is just and reasonable without the “final, populated project-specific schedule in Exhibit 1 for the B2H Project, including the final lease payment amount, SPE Lessor’s cost, and the net book value of the B2H Project,” which cannot be known until the B2H Project is actually completed. 
Taken together, these findings undermine the broader case for levelized rates.  The B2H 203 Order identifies deficiencies and rejects the Proposed Transaction based on factors that are not specific to PacifiCorp’s proposal.  Rather, these factors are inherent to the use of levelized rates as compared to COS rates, which will necessarily result in both (1) higher nominal costs and (2) periods in which the levelized rate will be higher than what customers otherwise would have paid.  These factors alone do not constitute an adverse impact on rates.  
First, the relative difference in the nominal dollar amount between a traditional COS rate versus a levelized rate is not the proper way to assess the rate impacts of a levelized rate structure that is designed, from the ground up, to be equivalent on an NPV basis.  NPV-based analysis is an economically sound way to set and compare different transmission rates to account for the time value of money to both transmission owners and transmission customers.  Just as a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in a decade, a well-designed NPV-based rate (as PacifiCorp has proposed here) holds both parties harmless by redistributing the timing of recovery and adjusting the charged rate accordingly.
Second, levelized rates are just that – level – while a traditional cost-of-service rate features higher rates in the early years and lower rates in the out years, reflecting the depreciation of the underlying asset and transmission owner’s recovery of its capital investment.  As a result, every levelized rate will be lower than an equivalent traditional COS rate in the early years, and higher in the later years.  The order addresses this inherent design element and concludes that “these features of the levelized approach could also be considered adverse to customers, such that the purported benefits may also create an adverse effect on rates….”  Again, this finding is not specific to PacifiCorp’s proposal.  If these factors constitute an adverse effect on rates, then every levelized rate proposal, regardless of how well-designed, will be presumptively harmful to customers as compared to the traditional COS construct.  
The net effect of these conclusions – that the combination of nominal dollar value increases and “higher” rates in the out years is sufficient to create an adverse rate effect for customers – is that, going forward, applicants will have a higher burden to justify the use of levelized rates over traditional COS rates.  Furthermore, this effect might not be limited to FPA section 203 proceedings and could easily bleed into our FPA section 205 precedent as well, if opponents cite the findings here to argue that levelized rates are harmful to customers.  These findings do not protect customers; instead, they may limit ways that utilities can help mitigate rate increases for customers in the near-term by using levelized rates.  Further, they could structurally bias our ratemaking against levelized rates, notwithstanding their potential benefits.  
Conclusion
Today’s orders create an unnecessary evidentiary hurdle to the use of levelized rate structures under both FPA sections 203 and 205.  I do not believe that hurdle is warranted based on the records before us.  Instead, I would have authorized the Proposed Transaction and accepted the Lease Agreement, while requiring that PacifiCorp submit a future FPA section 205 filing once the final B2H Project costs are known and the actual lease payments are calculated.  Going forward, I encourage applicants that propose levelized rate structures to bolster their filings with additional explanation of the benefits their proposals will provide, to ensure the Commission has a full record upon which it can assess those rates.   
For these reasons, I respectfully dissent.



Judy W. Chang
Commissioner
